title: Cicadas, grasshoppers, grubs and the other insects

names.gloss: locust, large cicada found in mountains

honey ant, the abdomen enlarges after eating

identification.basis: The dictionary names three cicadas, two grasshoppers, the cricket, two caterpillars, the edible case-moth larva, the honey ant, two beetles, the butterfly and the dragonfly, with the grubs on their own page. Roth and Palmer record which insects were eaten and how they were got.

summary: The dictionary knows its insects: **[yinja-yinja](word:yinja-yinja)** the cicada, **[dujandujan](word:dujandujan)** the 'locust, large cicada found in mountains', **[kurrmbal](word:kurrmbal)** 'species of cicada or locusts', **[jimu](word:jimu)** and **[yiljun](word:yiljun)** the grasshoppers, **[yijil-yijin](word:yijil-yijin)** the cricket, **[durra](word:durra)** and **[kinga](word:kinga)** the caterpillar, **[kuran](word:kuran)** 'larva of case moth, edible, found in green wood', **[jingka-jingka](word:jingka-jingka)** 'honey ant, the abdomen enlarges after eating', **[murrmun](word:murrmun)** the rhinoceros beetle and **[murrumun](word:murrumun)** the black beetle, **[walbul-walbul](word:walbul-walbul)** the butterfly, **[dijaraban](word:dijaraban)** and **[wurarr-wurarr](word:wurarr-wurarr)** the dragonfly, and **[jambun](word:jambun)**, 'grub, Mareeba dialect for *mujurr*', the one western word in the list [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's 1901 chapter on 'other insects, grubs, caterpillars' is short and plain: 'certain longicorn Coleoptera are eaten by the natives on the upper reaches of the Embley River. March flies are often treated similarly with by the Tully River children, etc. Grubs are hooked out of tree-butts and roots by means of the "feelers" of the lawyer cane, or else by sawing into soft and rotten timber with a piece of lawyer after the manner of a crosscut ... the blacks eat these grubs raw or roasted. In the Boulia and Cloncurry districts the smaller kinds of grubs and caterpillars, especially those found on grass, may be eaten raw and whole: the larger varieties, found in trees, are usually roasted, their heads not being eaten, or may be dried in the sun and put away for future occasions. E. Palmer states that on the Mitchell and Cloncurry the natives utilise a grub contained in the galls growing terminal on young trees of *Eucalyptus tetrodonta* and *E. corymbosa*', the stringybark and the bloodwood [ref:roth1901] [ref:palmer1883]. The best of the insect foods was a secret of the [green ants'](entry:green-ants) nest: 'the chrysalis of a lepidopteron, *Liphyra brassolis*, is found in the green-ant nests. The Bloomfield blacks, who call it *bi-i bi-i*, consider it a great delicacy', the caterpillar of the moth butterfly, which 'can devour the entire broods of green ant nests' under an orange armour the ants cannot bite through [ref:roth1901] [ref:wiki-liphyra]. The [witchetty grub](entry:witchetty-grub), the [green ants](entry:green-ants), the [native bees](entry:native-bees) and the [biting things](entry:bites-and-stings) have their own pages; this is the rest of the small life of [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters), the sound of the build-up and the food of every bird, lizard and fish on the river.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **Cicadas**: **[yinja-yinja](word:yinja-yinja)** 'cicada'; **[dujandujan](word:dujandujan)** 'locust, large cicada found in mountains'; **[kurrmbal](word:kurrmbal)** 'species of cicada or locusts'. **Grasshoppers**: **[jimu](word:jimu)** 'grasshopper'; **[yiljun](word:yiljun)** 'type of grasshopper'; **[yijil-yijin](word:yijil-yijin)** 'cricket'. **Caterpillars and grubs**: **[durra](word:durra)** 'caterpillar, worm'; **[kinga](word:kinga)** 'caterpillar'; **[kuran](word:kuran)** 'larva of case moth, edible. Found in green wood'; **[mujurr](word:mujurr)** 'witchetty grub found in rotting wood' and **[jambun](word:jambun)** 'grub. Mareeba dialect for *mujurr*'; **[ngirran](word:ngirran)** 'beetle fully developed from *mujurr*'; **[kurran](word:kurran)** 'kind of grub'; **[bikarrakal](word:bikarrakal)** 'a kind of grub used for bait'. **Beetles**: **[murrmun](word:murrmun)** 'rhinoceros beetle'; **[murrumun](word:murrumun)** 'black beetle'. **Ants and bees**: **[jingka-jingka](word:jingka-jingka)** 'honey ant, the abdomen enlarges after eating' (also 'silverfish'); **[dabadaba](word:dabadaba)** 'larvae and eggs of any kind of bee'; **[kurrmaja](word:kurrmaja)** 'larvae of green ants'; **[nyirran](word:nyirran)** 'the big green ant that is eaten, comes in December - January'. **Others**: **[walbul-walbul](word:walbul-walbul)** 'butterfly'; **[dijaraban](word:dijaraban)** 'mayfly, dragonfly'; **[wurarr-wurarr](word:wurarr-wurarr)** 'dragon fly'; **[biray](word:biray)** 'grey March fly' [ref:hershberger1982]. The Mareeba dialect word *jambun* is the one that belongs to the western side of the range, and the contribution box below is for the others.

sections.heading: The insects, and which were food
sections.body:
**Cicadas.** 'They have an exceptionally loud song, produced in most species by the rapid buckling and unbuckling of drum-like tymbals'; 'they typically live in trees, feeding on watery sap from xylem tissue, and laying their eggs in a slit in the bark. Most cicadas are cryptic. The vast majority of species are active during the day as adults, with some calling at dawn or dusk'; 'cicadas are eaten by humans in various parts of the world, including China, Myanmar, Malaysia, central Africa and parts of Mexico'; the nymphs live underground on root sap for years before the summer emergence [ref:wiki-cicada]. The dictionary's three cicada words and the empty brown shells on the trunks in the build-up are the north's version [ref:hershberger1982]. The sources used here record no eating of cicadas in Kuku Yalanji country.

**Grasshoppers.** 'Typically ground-dwelling insects with powerful hind legs which allow them to escape from threats by leaping vigorously'; 'they hatch from an egg into a nymph or "hopper" which undergoes five moults'; 'grasshoppers are plant-eaters'; 'at high population densities and under certain environmental conditions, some grasshopper species can change colour and behaviour and form swarms'; 'grasshoppers are diurnal insects'; 'they are used as food in countries such as Mexico and Indonesia' [ref:wiki-grasshopper]. Here they are the [kestrel's](entry:eagles-and-hawks), the [bee-eater's](entry:bush-birds), the [kookaburra's](entry:kookaburras-and-kingfishers) and the [frilled lizard's](entry:lizards) food, and the fish's when they fall in [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra] [ref:wiki-bee-eater].

**Grubs and caterpillars.** Roth: 'grubs are hooked out of tree-butts and roots by means of the "feelers" of the lawyer cane, or else by sawing into soft and rotten timber with a piece of lawyer after the manner of a crosscut. Both procedures are in vogue on the lower Tully, where the blacks eat these grubs raw or roasted. In the Boulia and Cloncurry districts the smaller kinds of grubs and caterpillars, especially those found on grass, may be eaten raw and whole: the larger varieties, found in trees, are usually roasted, their heads not being eaten, or may be dried in the sun and put away for future occasions. E. Palmer states that on the Mitchell and Cloncurry the natives utilise a grub contained in the galls growing terminal on young trees of *Eucalyptus tetrodonta* and *E. corymbosa*' [ref:roth1901] [ref:palmer1883]. The lawyer feeler for grubs is 'stripped of all its spikes but one — the one is left at the point — and is inserted in the hole made by the grub, and gently pushed down. The pliability of the feeler enables it to follow the bends and turnings of the hole until it reaches the grub' [ref:roth1904]. The big grubs are the larvae of the longhorn beetles and the wood moths: longhorn larvae 'are 0.5–22 cm long, elongated in shape', and 'all known longhorn beetle larvae feed on plant tissue such as stems, trunks, or roots of both herbaceous and woody plants, often in injured or weak trees' [ref:wiki-longicorn]. The [witchetty grub](entry:witchetty-grub) page has the dictionary's grubs in detail. The case moth's larva, *kuran*, 'edible, found in green wood', builds a case: 'the caterpillar larvae of Psychidae construct cases out of silk and environmental materials such as sand, soil, lichen, or plant materials. These cases are attached to rocks, trees or fences while resting or during their pupa stage, but are otherwise mobile'; in Madagascar one species 'is in some places encouraged to breed on wattle trees, because its pupae are collected as a protein-rich food' [ref:wiki-case-moth] [ref:hershberger1982].

**The moth butterfly in the green-ant nest.** Roth: 'it is interesting to note that on the Bloomfield, as well as at Cooktown, etc., the chrysalis of a lepidopteron, *Liphyra brassolis*, is found in the green-ant nests. The Bloomfield blacks, who call it *bi-i bi-i*, consider it a great delicacy, while the Cooktown natives, who speak of it as *ged-ya*, break it up in water, drink the mixture, and say it is very good for bad constipation' [ref:roth1901]. 'The larvae are predatory and feed on ant larvae. This is one of the largest species of lycaenid butterflies'; 'oval flattened and slug like with a hard and smooth covering. The caterpillars can devour the entire broods of green ant nests. The protective orange carapace is virtually impervious to the bites of soldier ants and it is so heavy that the ants cannot flip it over to get at the caterpillar's soft underbody. Once the caterpillar transforms into a butterfly inside the nest, its soft body is vulnerable to the ants ... it is protected by white scales from its new wings; the scales are slippery enough to prevent most ants from getting a foothold' [ref:wiki-liphyra]. Roth's *bi-i bi-i* is not in the dictionary, and the contribution box below is for it.

**Honey ants.** 'Honey ants are unique in using their own bodies as living storage, used later by their fellow ants when food is otherwise scarce. Designated worker ants, called "repletes," are the main group that store food for the colony. Repletes are fed by other worker ants until their abdomens become swollen with honey'; in the Australian *Camponotus inflatus* 'repletes formed 49% (516 ants) of a colony of 1063 ants'; 'the largest replete was 15 millimetres long and had a mass of 1.4 grams. The nest had a maximum depth of 1.7 metres', and the workers 'collect nectar from Mulga nectaries, and meat from the carcass of a *Tiliqua* blue-tongued lizard' [ref:wiki-honeypot-ant]. The dictionary's *jingka-jingka*, 'honey ant, the abdomen enlarges after eating', is the coast's knowledge of the inland's sweet; whether it was dug on the Mitchell is for the contribution box [ref:hershberger1982].

**Beetles.** The brown rhinoceros beetle, *murrmun*, 'can reach a length of 3.5–7 centimetres'; males 'have two chitinous bifurcated horns ... which they use to eliminate their rivals'; 'when disturbed these beetles make a hissing noise'; the larvae 'develop in decaying vegetable matter and usually take two years' [ref:wiki-rhino-beetle] [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's 'certain longicorn Coleoptera' eaten on the Embley are the adult longhorns [ref:roth1901] [ref:wiki-longicorn]. The dung beetles in the Karma Waters list are mostly the introduced ones that bury the cattle dung, with the native *Onthophagus* beside them [ref:ala-karma].

**Bee and wasp brood.** The dictionary's *dabadaba*, 'larvae and eggs of any kind of bee', and Roth's wasp larvae 'picked out and eaten raw' after the nest is smoked are on the [native bees](entry:native-bees) page [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Telling them
sections.body:
- **Cicada**: a fat, wide-headed, clear-winged bug on a trunk, screaming; its brown split shell on the bark [ref:wiki-cicada].
- **Grasshopper or locust**: long hind legs, jumps and flies a short way; the cricket is its night cousin [ref:wiki-grasshopper].
- **Witchetty grub**: a fat white larva in rotten wood; **case-moth larva**: a caterpillar inside a bag of silk and sticks hanging on a twig [ref:wiki-case-moth].
- **Moth-butterfly caterpillar**: a flat orange slug-shaped armoured thing inside a green-ant nest [ref:wiki-liphyra].
- **Honey ant**: an ant with a swollen clear abdomen, deep in a nest [ref:wiki-honeypot-ant].
- **Rhinoceros beetle**: big, shiny, horned, hissing when picked up [ref:wiki-rhino-beetle].
- **Dragonfly** (*dijaraban*): over the pool by day; **mayfly**: the same word in the dictionary [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Cicada shells on the trunks** and the roar at dusk: the build-up has come [ref:wiki-cicada].
- **A gall on a young stringybark or bloodwood**: a grub inside [ref:palmer1883] [ref:roth1901].
- **Sawdust at the base of a tree** or a round hole in a trunk: a longhorn or wood-moth grub [ref:wiki-longicorn].
- **A green-ant nest with a lump in it**: the moth butterfly's caterpillar [ref:wiki-liphyra].
- **Grasshoppers rising in clouds** before a walking person on the flat in the wet, and the bee-eaters and kestrels working them [ref:wiki-grasshopper] [ref:wiki-bee-eater].
- **Dragonflies over the pool**: the midges and mosquitoes they hunt are hatching.

sections.heading: Where they are
sections.body: The cicadas in the trees and their nymphs in the ground under them; the grasshoppers in the grass of the flats and the [woodland](entry:woodland); the grubs in the dead and dying wood and the galls; the honey ants in the sandy ground of the inland; the beetles in the rotting logs; the dragonflies and mayflies over the [waterhole](entry:waterhole) [ref:wiki-cicada] [ref:wiki-grasshopper] [ref:wiki-longicorn] [ref:wiki-honeypot-ant].

sections.heading: The base of the chain
sections.body: The insects are what the country's animals are made of: the grasshoppers and cicadas feed the [kookaburras](entry:kookaburras-and-kingfishers), the [bee-eaters](entry:bush-birds), the [kestrel](entry:eagles-and-hawks), the [lizards](entry:lizards) and the [frilled lizard](entry:lizards); the caterpillars and grubs the [honeyeaters](entry:bush-birds), the [quoll](entry:quolls-bandicoots-and-rats) and the [bandicoot](entry:quolls-bandicoots-and-rats); the night insects the [bats](entry:flying-foxes-and-bats) and the [frogs](entry:frogs); the ants and termites the [echidna](entry:echidna); and the insects that fall on the water the [archerfish](entry:archerfish-and-small-fish), the [saratoga](entry:saratoga) and the rainbowfish [ref:wiki-laughing-kookaburra] [ref:wiki-bee-eater] [ref:wiki-bfh] [ref:wiki-quoll] [ref:wiki-horseshoe-bat] [ref:wiki-echidna]. The grubs eat the dying trees and the beetles the dead ones, which is how the woodland's wood goes back into the ground [ref:wiki-longicorn] [ref:wiki-rhino-beetle].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: The cicadas and the grasshoppers come with the heat and the first rains; the flying termites with the first storms; the grubs are in the wood all year and the galls on the young trees after the wet growth; the big green ant *nyirran* 'comes in December - January' [ref:wiki-cicada] [ref:wiki-grasshopper] [ref:hershberger1982]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Food**: tree grubs roasted or sun-dried, grass caterpillars raw, the gall grubs, the moth-butterfly chrysalis, longhorn beetles, wasp and bee brood [ref:roth1901] [ref:palmer1883].
- **Bait**: *bikarrakal*, 'a kind of grub used for bait', and any grasshopper on a hook; see [hooks and lines](entry:hooks-and-lines) [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Medicine**: the Cooktown use of the moth-butterfly chrysalis in water 'for bad constipation', and the green ants; see [bush medicine](entry:bush-medicine) [ref:roth1901].
- **A clock**: the cicadas' roar for the build-up; see [seasons](entry:seasons) [ref:wiki-cicada].
- **A children's game**: *birray*, the March-fly chase; see [bites and stings](entry:bites-and-stings) [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Getting grubs with the lawyer feeler
sections.body:
From Roth [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1904]:

1. **Find the hole**: a round bore-hole in a trunk or root with fresh sawdust at it, or a gall on a young stringybark or bloodwood [ref:roth1901] [ref:palmer1883].
2. **Make the feeler**: a length of [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) 'stripped of all its spikes but one — the one is left at the point' [ref:roth1904].
3. **Push it gently down the hole** until it stops at the grub, then press and turn it for a few moments so the spike takes hold, and draw the grub out [ref:roth1904].
4. **Or saw the rotten wood open** with a piece of cane 'after the manner of a crosscut' [ref:roth1901].
5. **Eat raw or roast on the coals**, heads off the big ones, or dry the rest in the sun to carry [ref:roth1901].
6. **Gall grubs**: break the gall open and take the grub [ref:palmer1883].
7. **The moth butterfly**: look for the armoured lump in a green-ant nest when the nest is taken for its eggs; see [green ants](entry:green-ants) [ref:roth1901] [ref:wiki-liphyra].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Hairy caterpillars sting; 'if caterpillar hairs get stuck on your skin, remove them with tweezers or sticky tape' [ref:healthdirect-insect-bites].
- The green-ant nest fights back; see [green ants](entry:green-ants) [ref:wiki-oecophylla].
- The stingers and biters are on the [bites and stings](entry:bites-and-stings) page.
- Native insects are not protected wildlife in the way the vertebrates are, but the country they live on is; take what you eat.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The cicadas tell the Karma Waters build-up and the grasshoppers feed the station's birds; the grubs are in every dead ironbark [ref:wiki-cicada] [ref:ala-karma]. The dictionary's insect words are the coast's and one is Mareeba's; which insects were food on the Mitchell is for the contribution box below [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.body: *[yinja-yinja](word:yinja-yinja)*, *[dujandujan](word:dujandujan)*, *[kurrmbal](word:kurrmbal)* cicadas; *[jimu](word:jimu)*, *[yiljun](word:yiljun)* grasshoppers; *[yijil-yijin](word:yijil-yijin)* 'cricket'; *[durra](word:durra)*, *[kinga](word:kinga)* 'caterpillar'; *[kuran](word:kuran)* case-moth larva; *[mujurr](word:mujurr)*, *[jambun](word:jambun)* 'grub'; *[jingka-jingka](word:jingka-jingka)* 'honey ant'; *[murrmun](word:murrmun)* 'rhinoceros beetle'; *[walbul-walbul](word:walbul-walbul)* 'butterfly'; *[dijaraban](word:dijaraban)* 'mayfly, dragonfly'; *[minya](word:minya)* 'meat, eggs (protein food)' [ref:hershberger1982].
